citation: README.md desiderata (AI-native surface: configuration is files) and docs/architecture.md, the shape (config lives in the core). The format and every refusal here are Muster's own policy; there is no oracle above them.
why: This is the file a person types, and almost everything that can go wrong in it goes wrong silently. A daemon that never appears looks exactly like a daemon that is down, and a misspelled key looks exactly like a key that did nothing - so half of these cases are about what a refusal says rather than about what parses. The refusals are expected in full, not as codes, because the sentence is the deliverable: a taxonomy of error kinds would let the wording rot while every case still passed. Two policies are pinned here and are worth stating outright. A file is applied whole or not at all, because keeping the daemons that parsed would make a window's contents depend on which line had the typo. And an unknown key is refused rather than ignored, which is the opposite of what herdr's own socket API does - ignoring unknown params is why a `pane_id` misspelled for `target_pane_id` silently splits the wrong pane (docs/observations/herdr-0.8.0.md section 6).

cases.name: a file with nothing in it names no daemons
cases.why: An empty config is not an error, and will be the ordinary case the day this file holds only a keymap. It has to be distinguishable from a file that failed to parse, because the caller's answer to those differs: one means find the local daemon, the other means find the local daemon and say loudly that a file was ignored.

cases.name: a daemon needs only a name
cases.why: Someone running one herdr should have to say one thing. The socket is absent rather than defaulted here, because what gets written down is the wish - find whatever is on this machine - and a path found today is worth nothing to a run tomorrow (architecture.md, durability: persist intent, never observation).

cases.name: a socket path names one daemon out of several on a machine
cases.why: Two herdr daemons on one machine differ only by socket path, so this is the only way to say which. It is also the escape hatch for a daemon started with HERDR_SOCKET_PATH, which Muster's own discovery would otherwise have to be running under to find.

cases.name: a host makes a daemon remote
cases.why: Presence of `host` is the whole of local-versus-remote, and it is a destination ssh accepts rather than a hostname Muster parses. Everything about how to reach that destination - port, user, key, ProxyJump - belongs in the user's own ~/.ssh/config, where it already is for every other tool.

cases.name: ssh options are carried verbatim, for what a host alias cannot cover
cases.why: The escape hatch, and the reason the test fixture works: the devenv container's key lives in the repo rather than in anybody's ssh config. Passed through untouched because the moment Muster starts interpreting these it owns a worse copy of ssh's own option parsing.

cases.name: the order daemons are listed in is kept
cases.why: Regions are laid out in the order composition holds them and Muster owns no tree over them, so the file's order is the window's order left to right. A map keyed by name would lose it, and there would be nothing else to recover it from.

cases.name: a misspelled key is named rather than skipped
cases.why: The case this whole policy exists for. `hosts` for `host` produces a daemon that is silently local, which then fails to hold any of the panes the user expected, at a distance of several minutes from the typo. Refusing names the key while the file is still in front of them.

expect.refused: the first `[[daemon]]` block has a key called "hosts", which Muster does not read. None of the file was applied, because a key nobody reads is usually a misspelling of one somebody meant. Known keys here: id, socket, host, ssh_options.

cases.name: a keymap rebinds what it names
cases.why: Keyed by action rather than by chord, because an action has one chord and a menu item has one key equivalent - and because `split_right = "cmd+d"` is the direction somebody thinks in when they open the file to change a key they did not like.

cases.name: a keymap that names nothing leaves everything where it was
cases.why: Partial by design: a file that had to restate all fifteen bindings to change one is a file nobody edits twice, and it would silently drop an action the day Muster grows a sixteenth.

cases.name: an empty chord unbinds the action outright
cases.why: Different from not mentioning it. Somebody who wants their chord back for something else has to be able to say so, and the alternative is binding it to a key nobody presses and hoping.

cases.name: an action Muster does not have
cases.why: Almost always a misspelling of one it does, so the refusal lists them. Refusing the whole file rather than that line, on the same terms as every other unknown key here: a config half-applied is a config nobody can reason about.

expect.refused: `splitt_right` in the config file's [keymap] is not something Muster does, so none of the file was applied. What it does: new_tab, split_right, split_down, close_pane, next_pane, previous_pane, focus_left, focus_right, focus_up, focus_down, resize_left, resize_right, resize_up, resize_down, zoom.

cases.name: a chord Muster cannot read
cases.why: The other half of the same failure, and the one where naming the piece matters most - the refusal has to say which chord and what was wrong with it, or the answer is re-reading the whole file.

expect.refused: the config file binds `zoom` to `cmd+wat`, which Muster cannot read: `wat` is not a key Muster knows. Letters and digits are themselves, and the rest are spelled out: left, right, up, down, enter, tab, space, escape, backspace, delete, home, end, pageup, pagedown, f1 to f12. None of the file was applied.

cases.name: one bracket instead of two is the mistake worth catching by name
cases.why: `[daemon]` and `[[daemon]]` differ by one character and mean a table versus a list of them, and TOML accepts both. Without this the file parses, names no daemons, and looks exactly like an empty config.

expect.refused: the config file's `daemon` is not a list of blocks, so no daemon in it was applied. Each one is its own `[[daemon]]` block, with the double brackets - a single `[daemon]` declares one table and is the usual way to arrive here.

cases.name: a daemon with no name has nothing to be referred to by
cases.why: The id is not a fact about the daemon - herdr has no notion of its own identity - it is the name a region, a log line and a pane are attributed to. A daemon without one cannot be talked about, so there is no useful thing to do with the block.

expect.refused: the first `[[daemon]]` block has no `id`, so there is no name to refer to it by and none of the file was applied. An id is Muster's own name for a daemon rather than anything the daemon knows about itself - `local` and `devenv` read well in a log line, which is where they are met.

cases.name: two daemons cannot share a name, and the refusal says which two
cases.why: Names are how everything downstream tells daemons apart, including the pane ids that collide between them. Saying only that a name repeats leaves someone scrolling a file to find the second one, so the refusal describes both.

expect.refused: two daemons are called `work`, and a name is how everything else refers to one - a region, a log line, a pane that belongs to it. None of the file was applied. Rename one: the first is a daemon on this machine, the second is a daemon on devenv.

cases.name: ssh options with no host describe something that does not exist
cases.why: A local daemon reached over ssh is not a thing, and the likely intent is a `host` line that was deleted or never typed. Silently ignoring the options would attach a local daemon under a name the user expects to be remote.

expect.refused: the first `[[daemon]]` block sets `ssh_options` and no `host`, so it describes a daemon on this machine reached over ssh, which is not a thing. None of the file was applied. Add the `host` this was meant for, or drop the options.

cases.name: a value of the wrong type says what it found
cases.why: TOML makes 2222 a number and "2222" a string, and a port typed without quotes is the way into this. Naming what was found rather than only what was wanted is the difference between one edit and a guess.

expect.refused: the first `[[daemon]]` block sets `host` to a number, and it has to be a string. None of the file was applied.

cases.name: the block that is wrong is the block that is named
cases.why: A file with several daemons in it has several places a key can be wrong, and only one of them is. The ordinal is how someone finds it without counting blocks themselves.

expect.refused: the third `[[daemon]]` block has a key called "sock", which Muster does not read. None of the file was applied, because a key nobody reads is usually a misspelling of one somebody meant. Known keys here: id, socket, host, ssh_options.

cases.name: option composes characters unless the file says otherwise
cases.why: macOS's own behavior is the default, because it is what somebody typing accented text expects and Muster has no way to know which kind of typist it has. Stated as a case rather than assumed, since the cost of the default is that every alt chord an agent binds is dead until this key is set.

cases.name: option_as_alt names a side in the words a person writes
cases.why: `left` rather than `leftOnly`: the wire's spelling is right for a corpus and wrong for a hand-edited file, the same split the chord grammar already makes between `cmd` and `super`. The per-side values are the ones people actually pick, because option composes on macOS and a common arrangement is one side for meta chords with the other still composing.

cases.name: the wire's own spelling is read too
cases.why: A name copied out of a log line or a conformance case has to work in the file, or the two vocabularies drift and nobody can tell which one they are looking at.

cases.name: an option_as_alt Muster does not know says what it takes
cases.why: Silently defaulting to `never` here would produce exactly the symptom this key exists to fix, with a file on disk that looks like it fixed it. The refusal quotes the four names rather than saying `invalid value`, because the mistake is nearly always a near-miss.

expect.refused: `option_as_alt` in the config file is "leftonly", which Muster does not know, so none of the file was applied. It is one of `never`, `always`, `left`, `right`: `never` leaves option composing characters the way macOS does, and the others make that side of the keyboard send alt instead.

cases.name: a chord can stand for literal bytes
cases.why: The distinction an agent needs most and a terminal cannot always carry: shift+enter as a newline rather than as a carriage return. `[text]` is keyed by chord where `[keymap]` is keyed by action, and deliberately - an action has one chord so its name reads best, and text has no name at all, so the chord is the only thing left to key on.

cases.name: text bindings are read in a stable order
cases.why: Two runs over the same file must build the same keymap. A hash map over chords gives no such promise, and the day two bindings collide the winner would depend on the run rather than on the file.

cases.name: a text chord Muster cannot read is named rather than skipped
cases.why: The same policy the keymap already follows. A chord that silently did nothing is indistinguishable from a chord that is bound correctly and whose bytes went nowhere, and only one of those is the user's mistake to fix.

expect.refused: the config file's [text] has a chord `shift+enterr` which Muster cannot read: `enterr` is not a key Muster knows. Letters and digits are themselves, and the rest are spelled out: left, right, up, down, enter, tab, space, escape, backspace, delete, home, end, pageup, pagedown, f1 to f12. None of the file was applied.

cases.name: a text chord bound to nothing is refused rather than read as an unbinding
cases.why: `[keymap]` reads an empty chord as `unbind this action`, and the symmetry is tempting and wrong. There is nothing here to unbind: every default text binding is a chord no program asks for, so a file that wants one back binds it to the bytes it prefers. Refusing keeps the day that changes an explicit decision rather than a silent one already made.

expect.refused: the config file's [text] gives `shift+enter` an empty string, so pressing it would send nothing at all. None of the file was applied. Delete the line to leave the chord alone.

cases.name: two spellings of one chord cannot both be bound
cases.why: `shift+enter` and `enter+shift` are the same chord and TOML sees two keys, so one silently wins. Which one depends on the table's order, which is not something a person reading their own file can work out.

expect.refused: the config file's [text] binds `shift+enter` twice under different spellings, and one of them silently wins. None of the file was applied.
